# 40｜LLM 增强搜索抵御黑帽 SEO 的韧性：全文翻译与详细教学

原题：Unveiling the Resilience of LLM-Enhanced Search Engines against Black-Hat SEO Manipulation  
作者：Pei Chen、Geng Hong（通讯）、Xinyi Wu、Mengying Wu、Zixuan Zhu、Mingxuan Liu、Baojun Liu、Mi Zhang、Min Yang（通讯）。机构：复旦大学、中关村实验室、清华大学。完整作者邮箱见末尾原文第一页。  
版本：arXiv:2603.25500v1，2026 年 3 月 26 日；原文注明拟发表于 WWW 2026；本地 PDF 12 页。来源：https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.25500

> 这是一篇端到端搜索安全研究，不是黑帽增长操作指南。下文保留完整论文结构、表格、公式与附录；教学侧重正确测量、识别操纵和合规内容质量。本文中的历史产品数据和漏洞表现限于作者研究时的版本，本次没有在线复测。原文若有口径或算术疑点，均与译文分开标注。

## 一、全文中文翻译

### 摘要

大型语言模型增强搜索引擎（LLMSE）把网络规模搜索与 AI 总结结合，改变了信息检索。虽然这些系统相对传统搜索表现出更高效率，但其面对成熟黑帽搜索引擎优化攻击的安全影响仍未被研究。

本文首次系统研究针对 LLMSE 的 SEO 攻击。具体而言，考察 ChatGPT、Gemini 等十款代表产品，建立包含 1,000 个现实黑帽 SEO 网站的 SEO-Bench，评估开源与闭源系统。测量表明，LLMSE 能缓解超过 99.78% 的传统 SEO 攻击，其中检索阶段是主要过滤环节，拦截绝大多数恶意查询。进一步提出并评估七种 LLMSEO 策略，发现现成 LLMSE 对此存在脆弱性：改写查询堆砌和文本分段使操纵比例相较基线翻倍。本研究提供对 LLMSE 生态的深入安全分析，为更稳健的 AI 搜索提供见解，已向主要厂商负责任地报告问题。

CCS：安全与隐私——Web 应用安全。关键词：LLM 增强搜索引擎、搜索引擎优化、黑帽 SEO。

**图 1：传统搜索与 LLM 增强搜索比较。** 查询“LLMSE 的影响”，传统引擎返回 Gemini 页面、“LLM 如何影响工作”等分散结果；LLMSE 先分析搜索词、查找参考、总结回答，输出“搜索与 LLM 能力整合、用户体验改善、SEO 与内容策略转变”等带编号引用的概述。图中示例引用 dl.acm.org、wikipedia.org 等，只作工作流示意。

### 1 引言

在 LLM 新应用中，LLMSE 结合了网络的广泛搜索能力与对用户问题高效、准确的回答。由于其客观性及信息综合能力，它们越来越被视为传统搜索替代品。例如论文称 Perplexity 于 2025 年初按 180 亿美元估值融资 [7]。

图 1 比较两类搜索。用户输入实际问题，如“LLMSE 的影响”；传统搜索返回新闻、论坛等多个独立来源，而 LLMSE 直接生成结构清晰的回答，给出有组织的概览。

但 LLMSE 真的更可靠吗？包括黑帽 SEO 在内的搜索优化，多年来一直损害传统搜索结果质量 [10,32,35,43,47,64,67]。攻击者正转向 LLMSE，可能沿用旧手段或发明新操纵方法，使新系统面对性质不同的威胁，迫切需要理解与缓解。

**研究空白。** 现有 LLMSE 研究主要提升效率、准确性、可验证性 [39,42,57,65]；安全工作多关注模型级攻击 [1,45,54,70]。例如 PoisonedRAG 通过知识库投毒操纵 RAG，GEO 尝试文本优化以增加模型总结中的可见性。但这些方法通常在精心构造的设置中，只评估流程的部分组件，忽略现实端到端影响。Luo 等 [42] 观察到有害内容与恶意 URL，但未从传统 SEO 技术角度分析或评估各阶段弱点。传统黑帽 SEO 对 LLMSE 的影响仍探索不足。

**本研究。** 回答三问：RQ1，LLMSE 工作流是什么，其设计是否天然抵抗 SEO 操纵？RQ2，传统黑帽 SEO 是否影响 LLMSE，怎样影响各阶段？RQ3，有没有显著操纵 LLMSE 结果的专门策略？

首先分析十款热门产品工作流与攻击面；其次建立 1,000 个现实攻击的 SEO-Bench，评估开闭源防御并逐阶段分析；最后提出七种策略，以 450 个自行部署网站做端到端实验。问题均已负责任披露。

贡献：揭示现实产品多阶段工作流及攻击面；发现系统可抵抗超过 99.78% 传统黑帽攻击，主要由检索阶段过滤；发现改写查询堆砌、分段文本等 LLMSEO 策略可使操纵比例相较基线翻倍。

### 2 背景

#### 2.1 LLMSE 与黑帽 SEO

LLMSE 又称 AI 搜索，结合实时检索与生成式总结，已被广泛采用。论文引 Perplexity 月访问 1.69 亿 [56]，ChatGPT 2024 年正式加入搜索 [29]。相关研究考察效率、准确性、可验证性，也探索 GEO 可见性操纵及提示注入。

SEO 通常通过改进结构、内容、体验等正当手段提升排名与自然流量；黑帽 SEO 违反引擎规范，通过链接农场、关键词堆砌、搜索重定向、伪装、广告注入或术语混淆造成的语义混淆、长尾词攻击获取短期收益。

#### 2.2 威胁模型

攻击者为推广特定站点，故意改动结构或内容，使其更易被索引。受害用户输入某查询后，LLMSE 可能呈现站点，并把不可信链接纳入回答。

目标是诱使回答嵌入攻击者控制 URL。含链接输出直接引导用户到推广站点，因此研究关注含可点击目标域名引用的回答。能力假设：攻击者控制多个网站，可完全定制结构与内容，但不能访问 LLMSE 中间输出。

#### 3.2 攻击面

闭源系统通过主页、官方文档和人工交互观察；开源本地部署，检查输出和服务端日志暴露的中间处理。

**图 2：三阶段工作流及攻击面。** 理解阶段进行意图分析、查询改写；检索阶段用改写查询从搜索 API 或内部索引抓取并重排；总结阶段生成正文与引用。图示旧威胁包括关键词堆砌、语义混淆、长尾或无意义关键词、重定向、垃圾内容、链接农场；新威胁包括提示注入、改写查询堆砌、重排算法投毒、对抗文本劫持注意力。

第一阶段，理解查询：（1.1）意图分析推断需求、决定是否外部检索，如 ChatGPT、Gemini；过滤无关或恶意部分，抵抗无关堆词与语义混淆，但 LLM 推断仍可能受提示注入、越狱影响。（1.2）把输入改成一个或多个标准查询。所查十款中八款明确主动改写，常用角色扮演策略。它规范措辞，抵抗拼写变化、误导表达、长尾和无意义关键词；但若攻击者预测改写结果并据此堆词，也可能被利用。

第二阶段，检索：（2.1）用 Google、Tavily 等外部搜索或内部库抓取候选，一些系统可限可信域名；来源多样性减轻单一来源投毒。（2.2）对内容评分、按相关性过滤，排除链接农场等垃圾 SEO；评分启发式也可能无意偏向某些页面，第 4.4、5 节进一步研究。

第三阶段，总结：（3.1）综合连贯、一致回答，并通常提供正文引用与参考。除 ChatGPT、Gemini 外，多数依赖外部 LLM API，有些结合多个模型。它改善事实一致性并过滤垃圾、语义混淆内容，但仍可能受到劫持注意力的对抗文本影响。

### 4 对传统黑帽 SEO 的韧性

攻击者直觉上会把传统方法用于 LLMSE。本节用大规模现实黑帽样本评估，并拆解多阶段机制如何缓解或放大操纵。

#### 4.1 设置

选择 Google Search 代表传统搜索，收集现实中已成功的攻击。若在 Google 成功、在 LLMSE 失败，表示后者有韧性。使用已有攻击样本保证多样性并降低伦理影响。

**SEO-Bench。** 文献确定五类：语义混淆，把复制的合法文字与非法推广混合，稀释恶意意图以提升排名、避过滤器；重定向，利用高权威网站漏洞把用户转到推广目标，借用可信度；伪装，通过请求头识别爬虫，向搜索与用户呈现不同内容；堆词，过量或趋势词膨胀表面相关性；链接农场，大量互链低质量网站虚增权威。复现相应分类器并调试，见附录 A。

从既有研究提取 2,499 个涉及非法／禁止内容的词，从 2024 年 11 月至 2025 年 4 月 Google Trends 收集 9,301 个热词，共 11,800 查询。Google 每个取前 50 条，保存标题、摘要、URL、重定向链、HTML。原文称从“超过 500M 个收集网站”中识别 1,602 个有效查询—网站对，再每类选 200，形成 1,000 对。**原文 500M 与11,800×50数量明显不相容，未改成猜测数字。**

#### 4.2 全景结果

每查询每系统三次，共27,000请求。理解、检索、总结在各自阶段分别阻断15.7%、98.2%、85.2%，累计99.78%。检索过滤最多，总结追加防线，显示分层防御的重要性。

系统差异明显。ChatGPT 在该样本没有被任何传统攻击影响，拒绝率高；开源防御也很好，作者认为与 Tavily、SearXNG 等优化来源有关。Komo、Perplexity 受影响较大。

类型亦不同：语义混淆、伪装对最终输出风险最大；Komo 对语义混淆检索与总结过滤仅83.0%、73.5%；Gemini 只受语义混淆影响。重定向和伪装虽有些通过检索，很少通过总结；关键词堆砌对所评系统无影响。

发现 I：传统黑帽累计阻断99.78%，主要由检索过滤；语义混淆风险最大。

#### 4.3 理解阶段

意图拦截：通过 API 中是否调用 web_search 等字段检查，再人工核对拒绝的查询与回答。ChatGPT 有75.8%查询不产生引用，其中30.6%因安全政策拒绝，69.4%因把输入当陈述而非查询等意图误解。搜索作为辅助功能的系统可用内部知识回答时，往往不调用搜索。Gemini 拦截16.3%，其中67.4%拒绝、32.6%误解。此机制非专门反SEO，但可顺带在搜索前过滤有害／非法查询。

发现 II：ChatGPT 等意图拦截能过滤75.8%查询，即使并非有意反SEO，也在起点破坏操纵。

查询改写：从五款API提供改写查询的系统提取数据，几乎都倾向改写。图3是词数变化，GPT Researcher有77.56%扩展查询，其他更倾向缩短。系统提示表明前后缀、格式、语义丰富化由改善搜索准确性与体验的指令引导。

**图3：改写后的词数变化分布。** 五组为Gemini、GPT Researcher、Khoj、Open-WebUI、Storm；纵轴正值表示词数增加，负值减少，图保留分布而不反推精确原始样本。

补充实验把改写查询重新发给Google，98.16%不能找回原黑帽网站。即使编辑距离低于0.1，攻击成功也低于10%；说明轻微语法变化即可压低暴露，改写可成为轻量防御。

发现 III：改写可破坏长尾与堆词SEO，小改动也可把成功率降到10%以下。

#### 4.4 检索阶段

抓取偏好：用域名排名 [31] 分析趋势查询的返回链接。图4显示多数系统偏好高排名域名，前五千比低排名更常见；例如ChatGPT权威链接份额比Google近高50%。Khoj、Perplexica因幻觉URL有超过60%不可靠链接。权威偏好虽降低风险，但对高排名域名过度信任可能带来恶意重定向、评论攻击等新漏洞。

**图4：传统搜索与LLMSE检索引用的域名排名组成。** 从1、5千、1万、2万、5万、10万、50万、100万至更低档，按颜色显示各系统比例；不把排名高直接等同事实正确。

发现 IV：权威来源偏好改善质量，也强调高排名来源被攻陷的风险。

重排偏好：对同时出现在Google与LLMSE结果中的链接，按共同链接集合内的相对顺位计算：

\[

### 5 LLMSEO 攻击研究

基于上述发现，提出针对端到端流程的研究策略，超越只看排序或总结组件的既有工作。

#### 5.1 七种技术

理解阶段：改写查询堆砌，在网页大量加入可能的改写查询，因为系统未必使用原词检索，预测新查询可能提高匹配。提示注入虽重要，但已被广泛研究且高度依赖提示，因此排除。

检索阶段：内部链接，增加页面内链并连接关键页；多模态资源，加入文字、图片、视频提高丰富度和感知可信度；嵌套结构，采用结构化标签和索引，方便定位提取；文本分段，缩短独立文本块，使其更适合直接引用。

总结阶段：相关性增强，围绕核心词加强语义相关性与连贯性；问答格式，用类似LLM回答的对话式Q&A增加直接复用可能。以上是论文研究变量，不意味着这些正常编辑形式本身都是恶意；是否构成操纵取决于目的、真实性与使用情境。

#### 5.2 效果评估

方法：在受控域名部署博客，各推广同类产品的不同品牌。使用附录D域名限制提示请求推荐，记录推荐站点中各策略的比例。限制域名减少真实搜索污染并公平比较；出现多说明更贴合系统偏好。每系统重复查询10次、汇总出现次数；七策略加无SEO基线、传统语义混淆基线，共九类，每类50网站，合计450。全部标“仅供测试”，实验后下线。

### 6 讨论

安全意义：LLMSE改变用户信任与威胁环境。用户把生成总结、引用视为权威，过度依赖；恶意内容一旦进入可信输出，风险被放大。攻击者从传统黑帽转向适配内部偏好的系统级对抗。随着普及，弱点可能扭曲网络可信结构，需要及时稳健防御。

缓解：按阶段加强。理解阶段分析改写与意图解释稳定性，识别刻意迎合改写行为的输入；改述过滤可对抗RAG投毒，如PoisonedRAG所示。检索阶段不能只信静态域名权威，应结合重定向模式、跨查询引用一致性等行为信号，识别被滥用的可信来源。总结阶段防范检索页内提示或文本操纵造成偏差。此外通过链接来源、可信度指示等透明性减少过度信任，鼓励核验。

局限：十款代表产品按规模与热度选择，其他系统可能更强。伦理上策略被简化、部署时间有限，现实攻击可能更复杂持久；多策略联合作用未研究。

## 二、详细讲解：三个不能混在一起的“成功率”

### 1. 先看它在哪一道门发生

完整流程像三道门：理解用户要什么；找哪些资料；决定哪些资料写进答案。你的网站没被最终引用，可能在第一道就没触发搜索，也可能第二道没检索到，也可能已读取但第三道没采用。只看最终回答不能知道原因。

本文有价值的地方是拆开阶段。许多实验先把目标资料直接塞进模型，测得的只是最后一道门；这里的传统黑帽测试则保留真实检索环节，所以99.78%不能拿来反驳所有提示注入研究，它们测量的条件不同。

### 2. 阶段阻断率不能直接相加

教学例：1000次请求，理解拦截100，剩900；检索拦截90%即810，剩90；总结拦截50%即45，剩45。总阻断955/1000=95.5%，不是10%+90%+50%=150%。条件阻断率R₁、R₂、R₃合成时，剩余比例为(1−R₁)(1−R₂)(1−R₃)。

用论文平均值计算：1−(1−0.157)(1−0.982)(1−0.852)≈99.775%，接近99.78%。但这是把阶段平均值按流程合成的口径；若各系统分母不同、闭源中间阶段不可见，不应自动当成把27,000请求原始计数汇总后得到的精确总体比例。

### 3. 不搜索不一定是主动防御

ChatGPT拦截的查询中，作者称69.4%属于意图误解。把所有不联网都叫“安全识别成功”会夸大安全能力。一个助手不回答任何问题，也不会引用黑帽站，但它没有完成用户任务。防御评估必须同时看正常查询能否得到有用回答。

这里还存在口径差异：表3 ChatGPT未命中目标黑帽站，表5却报告总结引用与正文有2%非法比例。前者是命中特定目标站，后者是所有被分类非法内容的比例，并不是同一个事件；不能据前者写“绝对没有不安全来源”。

### 4. 表6最容易被误传

分段文本在某行占59.46%，意思是该行所有成功出现的站点中，59.46%来自分段组。它不是“做100个分段页面就有59.46个被引用”，也不是“每次开放网络提问有59.46%成功”。分母是成功出现的集合，而非全部攻击尝试。

更重要的是，提示明确限定site:{domain}。这像只让评委在作者自家展厅挑产品，不代表在整个互联网同真实品牌竞争的结果。它适合比较结构特征偏好，不能直接承诺真实获客增幅。

### 5. 页面特征差异不等于排名秘方

表4上升页面内链更多、DOM更深，是观察相关性。丰富内容可能本来就有更多章节、图片、链接，也可能来自不同站点类型。不能为了“DOM深13.93”而套很多无意义容器，也不能机械把每段减半就认定有收益。

正常内容可用清晰标题、完整段落、真实图片、相关内链帮助阅读。黑帽问题在于欺骗、虚假关联、制造伪权威，不在于“有问答”或“段落短”这些形式本身。教学只保留提高真实可读性、可验证性的部分。

## 三、原文校对疑点与边界

1. 数据量：11,800查询×50结果最多590,000结果条目，原文却称超过500M网站。除非另有未披露采集来源，否则数量不相容；不据此声称覆盖五亿网站。
2. 分类器表10：TP77、TN96、总200，准确率应86.5%，不是86.6%；F1=154/(154+23+4)≈85.08%，不是87.74%。五表按矩阵合计准确率91.1%，不是91.12%。保留原报告，注明复算。
3. 表12：合计成功1.46%，与98.16%失败对应的1.84%不同，分母关系未交代。
4. ED≤0.1总体9.52%低于10%，但STD≤0.1子格10.26%；因此“任何微小编辑都低于10%”不成立，应按所报告整体理解。
5. 表3链接农场累计行在检索后99.00%，若再按总结阻断79.2%合成，最终约99.792%，不是原表99.96%；需原始计数或作者说明。
6. 表5平均下降率75.3%、70.8%不是直接拿平均比例4.89、0.92、0.43做一次相除；不要混用平均条件率与总体比率。
7. 公式3、4分子未显式限定已进入阶段；实现时应使用同一条件集合。
8. 论文市场数据、2025年配置、测试时期结果不能替代当下产品评测。调查十款、传统测试九款、新策略表列七款，都是不同集合，不要统一说成十款都成功攻击。
9. 改写导致STD>0.5只表示在选用嵌入中的余弦为负，不足以证明自然语言必然逻辑矛盾；这是作者解释，不是逻辑定理。

## 四、小白实操：搭一张证据记录表

### 第一步：用自己的正常问题分清故障位置

假设你经营家居内容，问题是“租房不打孔怎么增加照明”。用已有搜索助手正常查询，记录完整问题、日期、产品版本、是否显示搜索、返回引用、最终正文。没有中间结果就写“不可观察”，不要猜它内部检索了什么。

选三种同义问法：“租房不打孔照明方案”“不能打孔的出租房如何补光”“不用固定墙面的客厅照明”。它们应保持需求一致，不能把“租房”误改成“装修新房”。比较来源变化，是观察稳定性，不是攻击平台。

### 第二步：核对引用，别只数品牌出现

逐条打开允许访问的来源，确认链接存在、内容真的支持对应句子、来源是否被重定向、最终落点是否与标题一致。对品牌比较，找型号、测试条件、日期与原始数据；一段“最好”宣传语不能作为客观依据。

记录列：问题、改写版本、最终引用、是否支持说法、是否存在异常跳转、内容日期、自己的判断依据。某网站排第一不自动证明权威，域名热门也不保证其评论区或被篡改子页可信。

### 第三步：把内容改得可理解，做小范围对照

拿自己的文章副本做两版。A保留原段落；B只把一个冗长段按真实子问题分开，加准确小标题，保持事实、来源、字数大体相同。让读者或本地已有工具检查是否更容易找到答案、是否遗漏限定条件。这里测试的是可读性，不是“攻击成功率”。

例子：原文把落地灯、台灯、灯带混成一段；改版分别解释摆放空间、是否需固定、已知参数及限制。不要为凑短段落删掉“不适合潮湿环境”等关键条件。Q&A只有在回答真实问题时才有意义。

### 第四步：对数据算一次分母

教学假设：一组页面被引用20次，另一组10次；总出现50次。第一组份额40%，第二组20%，前者份额是后者两倍。但如果第一组有200次尝试，第二组只有50次尝试，独立成功率分别10%、20%，结论反而相反。

所以每条百分比必须写“分子是什么、分母是什么、是否同样尝试次数、是否限域、是否重复同一问题”。没有分母的数据，不用来承诺商业效果。

### 第五步：给自有检索系统增加阶段日志

如果你维护自己的RAG或站内助手，可记录：原问题、改写查询、搜索是否执行、候选URL、重排前后位置、最终引用、拒答原因。日志不要包含用户秘密；敏感字段按实际权限处理。这样能区分资料未召回、重排淘汰、生成不采用。

防御候选包括检查重定向链、保持来源可追溯、把页面指令视为资料而非系统命令、对关键结论核对原文。每种防御都应同时测正常任务成功率，避免把“全部拒绝”误当完美安全。本文没有证明一套万能过滤规则。

### 第六步：对外讲解这篇论文的准确说法

可写：“研究在1,000个传统黑帽查询—网站对及所测历史配置中观察到较强端到端阻断，检索阶段贡献很大；另在受控域名比较中发现页面形式影响成功出现的组成。”

不要写：“AI搜索能永久免疫99.78%攻击”“所有模型都偏爱短段”“段落减半引用必翻倍”。这三句话都越过了实验边界。

with 1,000 real-world black-hat SEO attacks and then evaluated the
defense performance of open-source and closed-source LLMSEs
against these attacks. We further conducted a detailed empirical
analysis at different phases to uncover the preferences. Finally, we
propose seven LLMSEO strategies and conduct an end-to-end ex-
periment based on the 450 self-deployment websites. All identified
issues were responsibly disclosed to major LLMSE vendors.
Contribution. This work makes the following three contributions.
• We provide a detailed investigation of real-world LLMSE prod-
ucts, uncovering their multi-phase workflows and identifying
phase-specific attack surfaces.
• We reveal that the LLMSEs can resist over 99.78% traditional
black-hat SEO attacks, with the Retrieval phase serving as the pri-
mary filter, intercepting the vast majority of malicious queries.
• We report that LLMSEs are vulnerable to LLMSEO attacks, i.e.,
rewritten-query stuffing and segmented text, double the manip-
ulation rate compared to the baseline.
2
Background
2.1
LLMSE & Black-Hat SEO
LLMSE. LLM-enhanced search engines (LLMSEs), also known as
AI-powered search, combine real-time retrieval with generative
summarization and are now widely adopted. Perplexity reports
169M monthly visits [56], and ChatGPT officially added search ca-
pabilities in 2024 [29]. Prior work has examined their efficiency,
accuracy, and verifiability [39, 42, 57, 65], while adversarial stud-
ies explored visibility manipulation through GEO [1] and prompt
injection [45, 54].
Black-Hat SEO. Search Engine Optimization (SEO) refers to im-
proving website ranking and organic traffic through legitimate
means such as optimizing structure, content, and user experience.
In contrast, black-hat SEO manipulates rankings by violating search
engine guidelines, aiming for short-term gains through techniques
such as link farms [64], keyword stuffing [47], search redirection [32,
34], cloaking [60, 63], semantic confusion through ad injection or
jargon obfuscation [36, 67], and long-tail keyword attacks [35, 37].
2.2
Threat Model
Motivated to promote specific websites, the attacker deliberately
modifies the structure or content of the websites so they are favor-
ably indexed by search engines.. When a victim user inputs certain
queries, LLMSE may surface these websites and incorporate the
link to the untrusted website into the generated responses.
Attacker’s Goal. The attacker’s objective is to induce LLMSEs
to embed attacker-controlled URLs within their responses. Since
link-bearing outputs directly guide users to promoted sites, our
analysis focuses on responses containing clickable references to
attacker-controlled domains (e.g. citations).
Attacker’s Capability. We assumed that the attacker controls mul-
tiple websites and has full authority to customize both content and
structure. However, the attacker has no access to the intermediate
outputs of the LLMSE.

In this section, we surveyed the current popular LLMSE systems
across both open-source and closed-source markets. Through prac-
tical analysis, we can uncover the attack surface of each phase.
3.1

To gain a comprehensive understanding of the LLMSE ecosystem,
we systematically collected a list of actively deployed LLMSEs from
both industrial and open-source platforms. First, we searched key-
words such as “LLM search” and “AI search” via Google. We ex-
tracted products from the top 100 search results and selected the
five most frequently mentioned LLMSE products, which together
account for over 98% of the market [58], representing those with
the highest visibility and usage. Second, we surveyed popular open-
source repositories in “LLM search” and selected the top five LLMSE
projects with over 10k stars from Github [15], reflecting strong com-

We conduct a comprehensive analysis on the collected LLMSE

systematically reviewed their homepage descriptions and official
documentation, and manually interacted with them to observe user-
facing outputs. For open-source LLMSE, we deployed them locally
and analyzed their outputs and server-side logs to expose inter-

Phase 1: Understand the Query. LLMSE understands the user’s
input , and provide actionable guidance for subsequent phases. This
process contains two main components:
(1.1) Intent Analysis: Infer user intent and decide whether ex-
ternal retrieval is needed (e.g. ChatGPT [49], Gemini [19]). This
step filters irrelevant or malicious parts of the query, helping de-
fend against attacks like irrelevant keyword stuffing and semantic
confusion. However, LLM-driven inference remains susceptible to
adversarial attacks such as prompt injection or jailbreaks [40].
(1.2) Query Rewriting: Rewrite the user input into one or more
standardized queries [62]. Among the examined LLMSEs, 8/10
clearly indicate that they actively regenerate queries, often adopting
a role-playing strategy [14, 26]. This step helps normalize phrasing
and defend against adversarial manipulations based on typographic
variations or misleading phrasing, e.g. the long-tail SEO [35] and
non-sense keyword SEO [38]. However, it might be exploited if
attackers can predict rewritten queries and tailor stuffing attacks
accordingly, as further discussed in Section 5.
Phase 2: Retrieve the Information. In this phase, the LLMSE exe-
cutes the rewritten queries to gather candidate retrieved references
and their content for subsequent processing.
(2.1) Fetching: Employ external engines (e.g. Google [23], Tavily [59])
or inner database to fetch potentially relevant results. Some LLM-
SEs can restrict the search scope to curated domains [51, 52] to
improve reliability. The diversity of retrieval sources helps mitigate
single-source poisoning.
(2.2) Re-ranking: Scoring each retrieved content [19] and filter
for relevance. The re-ranking process filters out spam-driven SEO
abuse such as link farms, but its underlying scoring heuristics may
unintentionally bias page selection, which we further examine in
Section 4.4 and explore its attack implications in Section 5.
Phase 3: Summarize the Answer. After retrieval, LLMSE syn-
thesizes the summary and typically includes in-text citations or
references to enhance credibility.
(3.1) Summary Generation: Summarize a coherent and logically
consistent response. Apart from ChatGPT and Gemini, most LLM-
SEs rely on external LLM APIs for content synthesis [62], with some
integrating multiple LLMs [13]. It improves factual consistency and
filters out spam or semantic-confusion content, yet remains vulner-
able to adversarial text that can hijack model attention [45].

how traditional black-hat SEO affects LLMSEs and dissect how the

4.1
Experiment Setup
To evaluate the resilience of LLMSEs against black-hat SEO attacks,
we use Google Search as a representative traditional search engine
to collect real-world successful attacks. An attack succeeding on
Google but failing on an LLMSE indicates resilience. All samples
from existing attacks ensure both ethical compliance and diversity.
SEO-Bench Construction. To find black-hat SEO websites, we
first conducted a literature review, getting five categories of black-
hat SEO attack techniques that have well-established definitions:
❶Semantic Confusion: blends copied legitimate text with illicit pro-
motions to dilute malicious intent, which raises ranking and evades
filters; ❷Redirection: exploits vulnerabilities on high-authority sites
to forward users to promoted targets, thereby inheriting the trusted
site’s credibility; ❸Cloaking: detects crawlers via request headers
and serves SEO-optimized content to search engines while pre-
senting different promotional or unrelated content to real users; ❹
Keyword Stuffing: embeds excessive or trending terms to inflate ap-
parent relevance and manipulate ranking algorithms; ❺Link Farm:
creates large interlinked networks of low-quality sites to artificially
raise link-based authority scores. Based on these studies, we re-
produced the classification methods proposed in the corresponding
works and tuned the respective classifiers. The implementation and
evaluation are provided in Appendix A.
Then, we selected appropriate origin keyword queries, including
illegal-words and hot-words. Illegal-words typically involve terms
related to illegal or prohibited content, reflecting the underlying
incentives for black-hat SEO; we extracted 2,499 illegal-words from
prior studies [33, 36, 60, 67, 69]. Hot-words include popular search
terms unrelated to the actual page content, which attackers use to
boost visibility in rankings; we collected 9,301 hot-words from
Google Trends [18] over a six-month period (Nov. 2024 – Apr.
2025). We then queried these 11,800 keywords on Google, and saved
the top 50 search results, including their titles, summaries, URLs,
redirection chains, and HTML content. From over 500M collected
websites, we identified 1,602 valid query-website pairs by the
classifiers. To ensure a balanced representation of each attack type
in the dataset, we selected 200 pairs for each of the five SEO attack
categories. As a result, our SEO-Bench dataset consists of a total of
1,000 query-website pairs. Table 2 shows the dataset details.
LLMSE Defense Evaluation. We evaluate nine LLMSEs intro-
duced in Section 3, excluding Google AI Overview due to its limited
and unstable availability [17]. For closed-source LLMSEs, we select
their first version with full search functionalities, i.e., gpt-4o-mini,
gemini-1.5, sonar, komo. For open-source LLMSEs, we deploy
them locally with default configurations, and use gpt-4o-mini as
the summarization model to ensure comparability across systems.
To quantify the resilience of LLMSEs against black-hat SEO
attacks, we evaluate their ability to block target websites across
different phases. Each entry in SEO-Bench is a query–website pair
(𝑞𝑖,𝑡𝑖), where 𝑞𝑖is a search query and 𝑡𝑖is the associated black-
hat SEO website. We independently evaluate the resilience of each
phase using a phase-specific blocking rate, defined as the propor-
tion of attacks intercepted at that phase among those entering the
phase. Specifically: In Understanding phase, an attack is blocked if
the LLMSE decides not to proceed with retrieval after analyzing,
indicating an early rejection of the search. In Retrieval phase, an
attack is blocked if the LLMSE performs retrieval but the SEO web-
site does not appear in the retrieved results. In Summarizing phase,
an attack is blocked if the SEO website appears in the retrieval
reference but is excluded from the final reference. We also employ
Cumulative Resilience to intuitively capture the overall interception
achieved after each phase. The metrics are in Appendix B.
4.2
Landscape
We assess nine LLMSEs with three trials per query (27,000 requests).
Results are summarized in Table 3.
Our evaluation shows that LLMSEs are highly effective against
black-hat SEO attacks, with the Understanding, Retrieval, and Sum-
marizing phases blocking 15.7%, 98.2%, and 85.2% of attacks at their
respective phases. Overall, they achieve a cumulative blocking rate
of 99.78%, where Retrieval plays the most decisive role by filter-
ing the majority, and Summarizing adds a strong safeguard before
output generation. These results highlight the importance of lay-
ered defenses in LLM-based systems, enabling them to significantly
outperform traditional search engines in resisting SEO attacks.
Although the results show that black-hat SEO techniques can
still influence LLMSEs, the resilience varies significantly across
LLMSEs. ChatGPT is not affected by any black-hat SEO attack with
a high refusal rate. Notably, open-source LLMSEs keep great defense
performance, due to the fact that they choose the search engine
API such as Tavily [59] or SearXNG [55], which provide optimized
source. In contrast, Komo and Perplexity are most affected.
The impact of different types of black-hat SEO attacks on LLMSEs
varies as well. Semantic Confusion and cloaking pose the greatest
risks in the final output to LLMSEs. For example, Komo is severely
affected by Semantic Confusion, with a low filtering of 83.0% and
73.5%. Meanwhile, Gemini is only affected by Semantic Confusion.
In contrast, although both redirection and cloaking attacks have
successfully passed the Retrieval phase on some LLMSEs, few of
them advanced to the Summarizing phase, thus failing to achieve a
successful attack on the Summarizing phase. Besides, the Keyword
Stuffing poses no influence on any LLMSE.
▶Finding I: LLMSEs exhibit strong resilience to black-hat
SEO attacks, achieving the cumulative blocking rate of 99.78%.
Retrieval phase intercepts the vast majority of malicious queries.
Semantic Confusion poses the greatest risks to LLMSEs.

Intent Interception. Upon receiving a user query, LLMSEs infer
its intent to decide whether a web search is necessary. We ana-
lyze the interception mechanism by inspecting the specific API
field values, as ChatGPT and Gemini explicitly indicate whether
“web_search” is invoked. Then we manually check these refused
queries and corresponding answers. In our result, 75.8% of queries
on ChatGPT are intercepted with no reference. Among them, 30.6%
are refused due to violations of safety policies, and 69.4% are skipped
due to intent misinterpretation, where the system treats the input
as a statement rather than a search query. This is because, unlike
dedicated search engines, LLMSEs such as ChatGPT, which treat
search as an auxiliary function, tend not to invoke search when
they can answer based on internal knowledge. Similarly, Gemini
intercepts 16.3% of queries, with 67.4% refusals and 32.6% misinter-
pretations. Although intent interception is not designed to counter
SEO attacks, it can incidentally filter harmful or illicit queries before
search execution, thereby reducing exposure to malicious content.

GPT to filter out 75.8% of queries, effectively disrupting mali-
cious SEO attempts at the start, even though unintentionally.

phase, some LLMSEs generate a refined version of the original
query. To investigate how this step influences the effectiveness of
SEO-based manipulations, we extract the rewritten keywords on
five of the collected LLMSEs that provide the rewritten queries in
their API response, and compare them with the original inputs. Our
analysis reveals that almost all of them prefer to rewrite the query.
Figure 3 shows the changes in word count during the rewriting. For
example, GPT Researcher shows a strong tendency to expand the
query (77.56%), while others are more likely to shorten it. Further
examination of the system prompts indicates that the rewriting
mechanisms, such as prefix/suffix modifications, query formatting,
and targeted semantic enrichment, are guided by instructions aimed
at improving search accuracy and user experience.

black-hat SEO, we conducted a supplementary validation exper-

rewritten queries to Google Search showed that 98.16% failed to
retrieve the original SEO websites, with even minor edits (edit
distance below 0.1) reducing attack success rates to under 10%, con-

rankings. These results indicate that even slight syntactic modifica-
tions can substantially suppress exposure, suggesting that query
rewriting serves as an effective and lightweight countermeasure.

LLMSEO Attack
Building on these findings, we propose and evaluate novel end-to-
end attacks tailored to LLMSEs, extending beyond prior work that
focused only on ranking or summarization components [1, 2, 70].
5.1
LLMSEO Attack Techniques
As each phase of the LLMSE workflow (Understanding, Retrieval,
and Summarizing) exposes distinct security risks, we design phase-
specific LLMSEO attack strategies to systematically evaluate and
manipulate these vulnerabilities.
Attacking Understanding Phase. In this phase, rewriting intro-
duces ambiguity and susceptibility to manipulation. To exploit this
vulnerability, we design a targeted attack.
• Rewritten-query Stuffing. Embed potential rewritten queries ex-
tensively within web pages. Since most LLMSE may not always
use the original search key for retrieval (Section 3), predicting
possible new queries and inserting them in web content can
increase the likelihood of being matched.
Note that while prompt injection is an important attack vector in
this phase (see Section 3), its impact is well studied [5, 40, 45, 54] and
highly prompt-dependent, so we exclude it from our experiments.
Attacking Retrieval Phase. Aiming to increase the priority in
re-ranking and inspired by Finding V, we propose new techniques
designed to align with the scoring mechanism.
• Internal Links. Embed numerous internal links within web pages
to construct a network, simultaneously increasing the number
of links to key pages.
• Multi-modal Resources. Incorporate multi-modal resources (e.g.
text, images, and videos) into web pages to increase their rich-
ness and boost perceived credibility.
• Nested Structure. Use structured labels and indexing that are
better suited for retrieval to enhance the readability and accessi-
bility of content, helping LLMSE quickly locate and extract key
information, gaining an advantage in candidate selection.
• Segmented Text. Reduce the length of individual text segments.
Shorter texts are often more suitable for direct citation.
Attacking Summarizing Phase. To influence this phase, we de-
sign optimization strategies targeting both relevance and format.
• Relevance Enhancement. Focus on core keywords to enhance the
semantic relevance and coherence of the text to the query.
• Q&A Formatting. Present content in a question-and-answer (Q&A)
format in the conversational tone of LLM-generated responses,
increasing the likelihood of direct reuse by LLMSE.
5.2

To examine the applicability of these LLMSE attack techniques
influencing LLMSEs, we conducted a competitive experiment to
compare the efficacy of various attack strategies under real-world
conditions.

domain, each promoting a different brand of the same type of prod-

domain-restricted prompts (Appendix D), and recorded the propor-
tion of recommended sites associated with each attack technique.
This restriction reduces ethical concerns arising from real-world
search pollution while enabling fair comparison across techniques.
A higher occurrence suggests a stronger alignment between the
corresponding manipulation and the preferences of the LLMSE.

to the seven LLMSE attack types, we included one non-SEO and
one traditional SEO attack (i.e. Semantic confusion, which showed
the best performance in Section 4.2) for baseline comparison. For
each attack type, 50 websites were created. In total, the experiment

that, in Summarizing phase, LLMSE is more influenced by content
quality rather than the structure of external resources, underlining
the importance of content-level manipulation.
6
Discussion
Security Implications. The application of LLMSEs in information
retrieval reshapes user trust and the threat landscape of black-
hat SEO. Users over-rely on LLMSE-generated summaries and ref-
erences, perceiving them as authoritative, which magnifies the

risks when malicious content and links are included in trusted
outputs. Building upon traditional black-hat SEO, attackers are in-
creasingly adapting their strategies to the internal preferences of
LLMSEs, shifting content manipulation from isolated optimizations
to system-level adversarial interactions. As LLMSE adoption grows,
such weaknesses may gradually distort the Web’s credibility struc-
ture, highlighting the need for timely, robust defenses to support a
healthy information ecosystem and sustained user trust.
Mitigation. To mitigate the vulnerabilities identified in this study,
defenses for LLMSEs should be reinforced in a phase-aware manner
across the entire workflow. In the Understanding phase, analyz-
ing the stability of query rewriting and intent interpretation can
help detect inputs deliberately aligned with rewriting behaviors;
paraphrasing-based filtering, as shown in PoisonedRAG [70], can
counter poisoning attempts in RAG systems. During Retrieval, miti-
gation should go beyond static domain authority by incorporating
behavior-based signals, such as redirection patterns and cross-query
reference consistency, to identify abused high-credibility sources.
In the Summarizing phase, additional safeguards are needed against
prompt- or text-based manipulations embedded in retrieved pages
that may bias summarization preferences. Furthermore, user aware-
ness and transparency features, such as link provenance or credi-
bility indicators, are crucial to reduce over-reliance on generated
outputs and promote critical content verification, collectively en-
hancing the resilience of the LLMSE ecosystem.
Limitation. Our evaluation focused on ten representative LLMSEs
selected by user scale and popularity, though other systems beyond
this scope may demonstrate stronger resilience. For ethical reasons,
our implemented LLMSEO attacks were intentionally simplified and
deployed for limited durations; real-world adversaries may employ
more sophisticated or persistent methods, and the combined effects
of multiple strategies remain unexplored.
7
Conclusion
This work presents the first systematic security analysis of Large
Language Model-enhanced Search Engines (LLMSEs), revealing
how black-hat SEO continues to influence their behaviors. By ana-
lyzing phase-specific preferences and weaknesses, we demonstrate
effective LLMSEO attacks that exploit these vulnerabilities. We offer
insights into more secure and resilient AI-driven search systems.

cious web page classifier, used to predict the probability that a web
page is malicious, outputting prob_malicious. Both models are based
on the TextCNN architecture: Vocabulary Size = 10,000; Maximum
Sequence Length = 500; Embedding Dimension = 128; Convolution
